(vi) No such direction can be issued by any trial court to the Insurance Company to
pay and recover relating to liability in respect of a passenger travelling in a goods
vehicle after the decision in Baljit Kaur's case merely because the date of accident was
before such decision. The date of the accident is immaterial. Since the law has been
specifically clarified, no trial court is expected to decide contrary to such decision.
(vii) Where, however, the matter has already been decided by the trial court before
the decision in Baljit Kaur's case, it would be in the discretion of the appellate court,
depending upon the facts and circumstances of the case, whether the doctrine of "pay
and recover" should be applied or as to whether the claimant would be left to recover
the amount from the person liable i.e., the driver or the owner, as the case may be.
27. Now the discretion to pass direction to the insurance company to "pay and recover" remains
with the discretion of this Court. The claimants appeared to be poor village residents who had
already been engaged in the litigation right from 1996. If they are to execute the award for recovery
of compensation from the first respondent in the MCOPs, much time will be lost and they cannot
enjoy the fruits of the award. The object behind the direction to "pay and recover" is on a principle
that adjudication of their claims inte rse might delay the claim of the victims, as held in
Swaransingh's case supra. In order to shorten the litigation and as the claimants, being the
beneficiaries receiving the benefits flowing from the Motor Vehicles Act, a Social Welfare
Legislation, are entitled to get their compensation without undergoing cumbersome legal
proceedings, a direction of "pay and recover" is inevitable.

er to shorten the litigation and as the claimants, being the
beneficiaries receiving the benefits flowing from the Motor Vehicles Act, a Social Welfare
Legislation, are entitled to get their compensation without undergoing cumbersome legal
proceedings, a direction of "pay and recover" is inevitable. Bearing in mind the plight of the
claimants, under the circumstances available in these proceedings, this court is of the considered
view that the appellant be directed to pay the compensation first to claimants and to recover the
same from the owner of the vehicle/first respondent in the MCOPs.
28. As far as the quantum of compensation made available to each of the claimants is concerned,
this court does not find any infirmity in the observations of the Tribunal. The common award as to
the quantum of compensation is confirmed. The appellant insurance company is at liberty to
institute execution proceedings against the owner of the vehicle/first respondent in the MCOPs
directly before the court concerned as per the procedure set out in Nanjappa's case. With the above
said observations and directions, these civil miscellaneous appeals have to be disposed of and the
common award passed by the Tribunal is modified in this regard.
29. In the result, all the civil miscellaneous appeals are disposed of with the directions as contained
in this judgment. Consequently all the connected miscellaneous petitions are closed. Time for
deposit is eight weeks. No cost.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Bombay Bench At Aurangabad
payload.holding: The Tribunal erred in passing an order of 'pay and recover' against the insurance company when passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not third parties and their risk is not covered under the Act policy, and therefore the insurer is completely exonerated.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal or Court cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award and recover from the owner.

insurance company to pay compensation and then to recover it from the owner, but when the High

args.question: Defence of National Insurance Co. where the insured's truck driver had no valid driving licence — liability for death claim by deceased's family

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no driving licence at all. The Tribunal held the insurer proved a fundamental breach. The facts match your case — a truck (goods vehicle) driven without a valid licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest recent precedent (2024) establishing that a complete absence of a driving licence is a 'fundamental breach' that would ordinarily absolve the insurer. It confirms the legal principle we need.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of a tempo did not possess a valid and effective driving licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The Tribunal held there was intentional and wilful breach and granted recovery rights. The High Court upheld the pay-and-recover order.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment confirms that even where the insurer proves breach (no valid licence for a commercial vehicle), the remedy is pay-and-recover — not complete exoneration. It is the governing framework for your defence.
supporting.quote: The Claims Tribunal opined that since the driver was not competent to drive a transport/commercial vehicle, there was intentional and wilful breach of the terms and conditions of the policy and thus, while making the Insurance Company liable to pay the compensation initially also granted it recovery rights.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions permitting the insurer to pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). The court held this was a breach and directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves a truck — a transport vehicle — where the driver had no licence at all, which is an even stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that driving a transport vehicle without the proper class of licence is a breach. The court exhaustively analysed the distinction between LMV and transport vehicle licences under the MV Act and Rules.
supporting.quote: A person holding a driving licence to ply 'light motor vehicle' cannot ply 'transport vehicle'... The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport endorsement but no separate endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle (16,200 kg lorry). The court held the insurer must pay and recover. Your case involves a truck with no licence at all — a stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a mismatch between licence class and vehicle type (let alone no licence at all) entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The court applied Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the lorry has been granted licence to drive one type of vehicle, but at the relevant time the driver was driving another type of vehicle... the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach of insurance policy terms entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for hazardous goods on a tanker. The court reversed the Tribunal's finding of valid licence and granted pay-and-recover. Your case involves a complete absence of licence — a more fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that courts will find a breach even where the driver held a licence for the general class of vehicle but lacked a specific endorsement. The principle extends a fortiori to a case with no licence at all.
supporting.quote: Therefore, he was not competent to drive Truck/Tanker and there is clear cut violation of the terms and conditions of insurance policy... the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed only after the accident. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves no licence at all — a stronger position.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a temporary lapse in licence validity (expired but later renewed) constitutes a breach. The court applied Ram Babu Tiwari and Section 15 of the MV Act.
supporting.quote: The admitted position is that as on the date of accident, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not having valid and effective driving license.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: When a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision of the Karnataka High Court consolidates the law on pay-and-recover. It discusses cases where the driver did not possess a valid driving licence and holds that the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive analysis of the pay-and-recover doctrine in the corpus. It resolves the conflict between earlier Division Bench decisions and confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves a fundamental breach (including no licence), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that the absence of a specific endorsement or badge does not amount to a fundamental breach, and the insurer remains liable. They will argue that if a driver with an LMV licence driving a commercial vehicle is covered, then a fortiori the insurer must pay.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the driver there held a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. In your case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself in Swaran Singh (cited in Iyyapan) distinguished between 'no licence' and 'licence for a different class'. Iyyapan expressly says 'the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle' — that is the critical difference.
adverse.quote: In the instant case, admittedly the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle. There is no dispute that the motor vehicle in question... was Mahindra Maxi Cab. Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will argue that an expired licence (which was later renewed) is analogous to 'no licence' — both involve driving without a current valid licence. They will cite this to say the breach is not 'fundamental' and the insurer must pay without recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case deals with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — the driver had held a valid licence historically. The court reasoned that the driver was 'authorised to drive' and the expiry was a technicality. In your case, the driver had NO licence at any point. The distinction between 'no licence ever' and 'licence expired but later renewed' is well-recognised in Swaran Singh and Laxmi Narain Dhut. Furthermore, this is a 2001 Tribunal decision, not binding on higher courts.
adverse.quote: It is clear that mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy.

adverse.title: L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav
adverse.principle: Section 167 of the Motor Vehicles Act does not bar a claimant from maintaining a claim petition against a third-party tortfeasor under the MV Act merely because compensation was previously sought from the employer under the Workmen's Compensation Act. Also, the insurer must prove the licence was fake with cogent evidence.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant may cite this for the proposition that the insurer bears a heavy burden to prove the licence was fake or invalid, and that mere non-production of the licence by the owner does not discharge this burden. The court held the insurer failed to prove the licence was fake.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In this case, the insurer alleged the licence was 'fake' but failed to lead cogent evidence — the investigation report was not properly proved. In your case, if the driver had NO licence at all (not a fake one), the burden is different: the absence of a licence can be proved through the charge sheet, the owner's failure to produce it, and the driver's own admission or non-appearance. The court in doc_005 itself noted the insurer must prove 'fundamental breach' — complete absence of any licence is inherently a fundamental breach.
adverse.quote: The Insurance Company could not prove, that the driving license in question was fake, by leading the cogent evidence on record. Secondly, if for the sake of argument, it is presumed that license was fake, even the Insurance Company could not prove on record that the factum of fake license was within the knowledge of the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this for the straightforward proposition that even with no valid licence, the insurer must pay and recover — they will argue this is the settled law and the insurer cannot avoid payment altogether.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover framework, not complete exoneration. It confirms the insurer's right to recover from the owner. The risk is low because it does not undermine the defence — it merely confirms the remedy is pay-and-recover, which is exactly what we are prepared for. The court applied S. Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
adverse.quote: Even if the offending vehicle was being driven by the driver having no valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further insurer has a right to recover the amount of compensation from the insured i.e. owner of the offending vehicle.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet, and 50% deduction may be applied.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant may argue that this case shows that driving without a licence goes to contributory negligence of the victim, not to the insurer's liability. They may try to limit the relevance of 'no licence' to contributory negligence rather than breach of policy.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This was an injury case where the claimant himself was driving without a licence — the 'no licence' went to his own contributory negligence. In your case, the deceased was a third-party victim (not the driver), so this principle does not apply. The absence of the driver's licence goes to policy breach, not contributory negligence of the deceased.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed... he did not have DL at the time of accident.

adverse.title: Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P
adverse.principle: Absence of a driving licence does not in itself constitute rashness or negligence in driving for criminal liability under Sections 279/337/338 IPC.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant may argue that the absence of a licence is irrelevant to the question of negligence — the accident could still have occurred even with a licensed driver. This could undermine arguments that the breach caused the accident.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a criminal revision case about rash and negligent driving under the IPC — not a civil compensation case under the MV Act. The standard of proof and the legal issues are entirely different. In civil claims under Section 166 MV Act, the breach of policy conditions (no licence) is relevant to the insurer's liability under Section 149(2), not to whether the driver was negligent. The two inquiries are separate.
adverse.quote: It was laid down... that absence of a driving licence does not constitute rashness or negligence.

priority_arguments: 1. The driver had NO valid driving licence at all — this is a 'fundamental breach' under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act, as held in Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) and Satto (doc_033). The complete absence of a licence is the strongest category of breach, distinguishable from cases involving expired licences (doc_034) or missing endorsements (doc_032).

2. The burden of proving the breach is on the insurer, but it is discharged by: (a) the charge sheet showing the driver had no licence; (b) the owner's failure to produce the driving licence; (c) the driver's non-appearance or admission. See doc_024 where the Tribunal drew an adverse inference from non-production.

3. Even if the Tribunal directs pay-and-recover (which is the likely outcome), the insurer must secure an express recovery right against the owner. The Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) confirms this is available even for Act policies.

4. If the deceased was a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (truck), the insurer may argue no statutory liability at all under Section 147 — see doc_014 (Shivlal) and doc_028 (Sukumarbai). However, this depends on the facts of how the deceased was travelling.

5. Quantum: If liability is established, argue for deduction of 50% towards personal expenses if the deceased was a bachelor (Sarla Verma), and no future prospects if the deceased was self-employed above 40. Use the compute_quantum tool for precise figures.
strategy.compensation_range: If liability is established, the compensation will depend on the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. Without those facts, a precise range cannot be given. However, the corpus shows typical awards for death claims range from approximately Rs. 5-25 lakhs depending on the deceased's income and age. Use compute_quantum once the deceased's particulars are known.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. Key variables: (1) monthly income (to be proved by the claimants); (2) age of deceased (determines multiplier); (3) number of dependents (determines dependency deduction — 1/3rd for 2-3 dependents, 1/4th for 4+, 1/2 for 1 dependent); (4) future prospects (25% if self-employed below 40, 40% if employed below 40, 15% if self-employed between 40-50, 10% if between 50-60, nil if above 60); (5) conventional heads (Rs. 70,000 under Pranay Sethi as updated).
risks: 1. The Tribunal may direct pay-and-recover rather than complete exoneration — this is the near-certain outcome for third-party claims. The insurer should be prepared for this and ensure the recovery right is explicitly recorded.

2. If the claimants prove that the owner made reasonable enquiries and believed the driver had a licence, the breach may not be 'fundamental' — see doc_005 (Bindudevi) citing Hind Samachar. The insurer must probe whether the owner exercised due diligence.
3. If the deceased was travelling as an owner of goods in the truck, the insurer may still be liable under Section 147 — the 'gratuitous passenger' defence (doc_014, doc_028) may not apply.
4. The claimant will cite S. Iyyapan (doc_032) and Swaran Singh to argue that the insurer must pay even with no licence — this is correct law, but the insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner.
5. If the insurer fails to lead proper evidence (e.g., examining the RTO official, producing the driving licence verification report), the breach may not be held proved — see doc_005.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: The matter will proceed before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be: (a) a finding that the driver had no valid driving licence, constituting a fundamental breach of policy conditions; (b) an order directing the insurer to pay the award and recover the same from the insured owner (pay-and-recover); (c) alternatively, if the facts permit (e.g., gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle), complete exoneration. The insurer should also consider filing a separate recovery proceeding against the owner after satisfying the award.

caveats: 1. This corpus does not contain the Supreme Court's landmark judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, which is the foundational authority on this subject. You must read Swaran Singh separately — it is cited extensively in nearly every judgment in this corpus.

2. The corpus does not contain the Supreme Court's judgment in Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba (2018) or Shamanna v. Divisional Manager, Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd., which are cited in some of the judgments. These should be consulted separately.

3. The corpus contains judgments from multiple unrelated fields (trademark, specific performance, criminal NI Act, etc.) — these have been excluded from the analysis as irrelevant to the motor accident compensation question.
4. The quantum of compensation cannot be estimated without knowing the deceased's age, income, occupation, and number of dependents. Use the compute_quantum tool once these facts are available.

5. The criminal revision case (doc_016) holding that absence of a licence does not constitute negligence is from a criminal proceeding and is not binding on the civil Tribunal — but the claimant may still cite it.

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

an attachment made to the prime mover of tractor and it has no independent driving system.
Therefore, it is not required to be insured under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and

trailer always is a detachable container, which does not have any independent driving system. Its
movements are dependent on the prime mover, such as tractor, motor vehicle etc. Hence, insurance
of trailer is not a mandatory requirement under the provisions of Section 146 of Motor Vehicles Act
and if the prime mover/motor vehicle/tractor is insured and the negligence of the driver of the said
motor vehicle is established, the compensation is payable by the owner of the tractor and insurer
irrespective of the fact whether the victim suffers injury with the tractor or with the trailer.
Therefore, we are of the view that in such cases, the insurance company is also liable along with the
owner of the tractor/trailer to pay compensation.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Punjab & Haryana At Chandigarh
payload.holding: The criminal revision petition is partly allowed by upholding the conviction of the petitioner under Sections 279, 337, 304-A, and 427 of the IPC, but modifying the substantive sentence for the offence under Section 304-A IPC from two years of rigorous imprisonment to 18 months, while maintaining the other sentences and fine.
payload.ratio: In-court identification by eyewitnesses is valid and admissible in law even without a prior Test Identification Parade, provided the witnesses had sufficient opportunity to observe the accused. Furthermore, discontinuation of medical treatment or shifting hospitals by a victim does not break the causal link between the accident injuries and death unless supported by medical evidence showing improper care or material alteration of treatment.

rashness and negligence on part of the accused.

Court is of the considered view that
the prosecution has successfully proved the identity of the accused beyond reasonable

The prosecution has to prove that that the negligence or rashness of the accused went

the Apex Court has held that:
"It is wrong proposition that for any motor accident, negligence of driver should be
presumed. To constitute either of the offence under section 279 IPC or section 304-A
IPC, the proof of criminal rashness or criminal negligence is essential. Even in
ordinary parlance 'negligence' connotes want of proper care and 'rashness' conveys
the idea of recklessness or doing of an act without due consideration. The rashness or
negligence must be described as criminal rashness or criminal negligence. "

the side of the road, an area typically used by pedestrians.

headlights and indicators, a damaged bumper, bent mudguard, shattered windscreen, and damage

22 of 32 CRR-2406-2025 (O&M) The petitioner could not explain how such damage had been

27. The contention of the petitioner disputing his identification as the driver of the offending vehicle
is thus wholly untenable. The law is well settled that the testimony of witnesses cannot be discarded
merely on the ground that they are related to the deceased. While Courts remain circumspect in
evaluating such testimony, the mere fact of relationship cannot be a ground to discredit witnesses.
PW-6 was the son of the deceased, assisting his father in his daily vocation, while PW-7 was a
neighbouring shopkeeper. Their presence at the spot was most natural, and no evidence of prior
enmity, bias, or mala fides has been brought on record to cast doubt on their depositions.
28. The site plan further fortifies the prosecution case. The deceased was standing towards the

accident demonstrates negligence on part of the driver. The deceased, who was merely standing off
the road, cannot by any stretch be attributed contributory negligence.
29. In so far as the plea regarding non-establishment of the petitioner's identity is concerned, the
same deserves outright rejection.

payload.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
payload.court: In The High Court Of Gujarat At Ahmedabad
payload.holding: The Court held that where passengers carried in a goods vehicle or tractor are gratuitous passengers whose risk is neither covered by statute nor by the insurance policy, the Claims Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4) and (5) to direct the insurance company to first pay the compensation and then recover it from the owner.
payload.ratio: In cases where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the terms of the insurance policy (such as gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle), the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act are not attracted, and neither the Claims Tribunal nor the High Court has the power to direct the insurer to pay the compensation and recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no driving licence at all. The Tribunal held the insurer proved a fundamental breach. The facts match your case — a goods vehicle driven without any valid licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest recent precedent (2024) establishing that a complete absence of a driving licence is a 'fundamental breach' that would ordinarily absolve the insurer. It confirms the legal principle we need.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of a tempo did not possess a valid and effective driving licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The Tribunal held there was intentional and wilful breach and granted recovery rights. The High Court upheld the pay-and-recover order.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment confirms that even where the insurer proves breach (no valid licence for a commercial vehicle), the remedy is pay-and-recover — not complete exoneration. It is the governing framework for your defence.
supporting.quote: The Claims Tribunal opined that since the driver was not competent to drive a transport/commercial vehicle, there was intentional and wilful breach of the terms and conditions of the policy and thus, while making the Insurance Company liable to pay the compensation initially also granted it recovery rights.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions permitting the insurer to pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). The court held this was a breach and directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves a truck — a transport vehicle — where the driver had no licence at all, which is an even stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that driving a transport vehicle without the proper class of licence is a breach. The court exhaustively analysed the distinction between LMV and transport vehicle licences under the MV Act and Rules.
supporting.quote: A person holding a driving licence to ply 'light motor vehicle' cannot ply 'transport vehicle'... The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: When a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision of the Karnataka High Court consolidates the law on pay-and-recover. It discusses cases where the driver did not possess a valid driving licence and holds that the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive analysis of the pay-and-recover doctrine in the corpus. It resolves the conflict between earlier Division Bench decisions and confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves a fundamental breach (including no licence), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport endorsement but no separate endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle (16,200 kg lorry). The court held the insurer must pay and recover. Your case involves a truck with no licence at all — a stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a mismatch between licence class and vehicle type (let alone no licence at all) entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The court applied Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the lorry has been granted licence to drive one type of vehicle, but at the relevant time the driver was driving another type of vehicle... the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach of insurance policy terms entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for hazardous goods on a tanker. The court reversed the Tribunal's finding of valid licence and granted pay-and-recover. Your case involves a complete absence of licence — a more fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that courts will find a breach even where the driver held a licence for the general class of vehicle but lacked a specific endorsement. The principle extends a fortiori to a case with no licence at all.
supporting.quote: Therefore, he was not competent to drive Truck/Tanker and there is clear cut violation of the terms and conditions of insurance policy... the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed only after the accident. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves no licence at all — a stronger position.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a temporary lapse in licence validity (expired but later renewed) constitutes a breach. The court applied Ram Babu Tiwari and Section 15 of the MV Act.
supporting.quote: The admitted position is that as on the date of accident, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not having valid and effective driving license.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In third-party cases, the insurer must indemnify and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Supreme Court judgment confirms that for third-party claims (like your death claim), the insurer must pay and recover. It also holds that a fake licence cannot be cured by renewal — relevant if the licence turns out to be fake rather than simply absent.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority confirming the pay-and-recover framework for third-party claims. It also establishes that a fake licence is a more serious breach than an expired one.
supporting.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that the absence of a specific endorsement or badge does not amount to a fundamental breach, and the insurer remains liable. They will argue that if a driver with an LMV licence driving a commercial vehicle is covered, then a fortiori the insurer must pay where the driver had some licence (even if not the right class). They will also rely on the broad proposition that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided for licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the driver there held a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest recent precedent (2024) establishing that a complete absence of a driving licence is a 'fundamental breach' that would ordinarily absolve the insurer. It confirms the legal principle we need.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision of the Karnataka High Court consolidates the law on pay-and-recover. It discusses cases where the driver did not possess a valid driving licence and holds that the insurer must pay and recover.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others

supporting.quote: Therefore, he was not competent to drive Truck/Tanker and there is clear cut violation of the terms and conditions of insurance policy... the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. result.question: Defence of National Insurance Co. where the insured's truck driver had no valid driving licence — liability for death claim by deceased's family

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no driving licence at all. The Tribunal held the insurer proved a fundamental breach. The facts match your case — a goods vehicle driven without any valid licence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest recent precedent (2024) establishing that a complete absence of a driving licence is a 'fundamental breach' that would ordinarily absolve the insurer. It confirms the legal principle we need.
supporting.quote: Hence, it is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of a tempo did not possess a valid and effective driving licence to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The Tribunal held there was intentional and wilful breach and granted recovery rights. The High Court upheld the pay-and-recover order.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Delhi High Court judgment confirms that even where the insurer proves breach (no valid licence for a commercial vehicle), the remedy is pay-and-recover — not complete exoneration. It is the governing framework for your defence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions permitting the insurer to pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). The court held this was a breach and directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves a truck — a transport vehicle — where the driver had no licence at all, which is an even stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that driving a transport vehicle without the proper class of licence is a breach. The court exhaustively analysed the distinction between LMV and transport vehicle licences under the MV Act and Rules.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: When a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Full Bench decision of the Karnataka High Court consolidates the law on pay-and-recover. It discusses cases where the driver did not possess a valid driving licence and holds that the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive analysis of the pay-and-recover doctrine in the corpus. It resolves the conflict between earlier Division Bench decisions and confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves a fundamental breach (including no licence), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In third-party cases, the insurer must indemnify and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: This Supreme Court judgment confirms that for third-party claims (like your death claim), the insurer must pay and recover. It also holds that a fake licence cannot be cured by renewal — relevant if the licence turns out to be fake rather than simply absent.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority confirming the pay-and-recover framework for third-party claims. It also establishes that a fake licence is a more serious breach than an expired one.
supporting.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport endorsement but no separate endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle (16,200 kg lorry). The court held the insurer must pay and recover. Your case involves a truck with no licence at all — a stronger breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a mismatch between licence class and vehicle type (let alone no licence at all) entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The court applied Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach of insurance policy terms entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for hazardous goods on a tanker. The court reversed the Tribunal's finding of valid licence and granted pay-and-recover. Your case involves a complete absence of licence — a more fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that courts will find a breach even where the driver held a licence for the general class of vehicle but lacked a specific endorsement. The principle extends a fortiori to a case with no licence at all.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired and was renewed only after the accident. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date but directed pay-and-recover. Your case involves no licence at all — a stronger position.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even a temporary lapse in licence validity (expired but later renewed) constitutes a breach. The court applied Ram Babu Tiwari and Section 15 of the MV Act.
supporting.quote: The admitted position is that as on the date of accident, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not having valid and effective driving license.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this Supreme Court judgment to argue that the absence of a specific endorsement or badge does not amount to a fundamental breach, and the insurer remains liable. They will argue that if a driver with an LMV licence driving a commercial vehicle is covered, then a fortiori the insurer must pay where the driver had some licence (even if not the right class). They will also rely on the broad proposition that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be avoided for licence defects.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the driver there held a valid LMV licence — the dispute was only about the absence of an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. The Supreme Court itself in Swaran Singh (cited in Iyyapan) distinguished between 'no licence' and 'licence for a different class'. Iyyapan expressly says 'the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle' — that is the critical difference. In your case, the driver had NO licence at all. The complete absence of any licence is a fundamentally different category of breach.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will argue that an expired licence (which was later renewed) is analogous to 'no licence' — both involve driving without a current valid licence. They will cite this to say the breach is not 'fundamental' and the insurer must pay without recovery rights, or at least that the breach is not so fundamental as to justify anything beyond pay-and-recover.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case deals with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — the driver had held a valid licence historically. The court reasoned that the driver was 'authorised to drive' and the expiry was a technicality. In your case, the driver had NO licence at any point. The distinction between 'no licence ever' and 'licence expired but later renewed' is well-recognised in Swaran Singh and Laxmi Narain Dhut. Furthermore, this is a 2001 Tribunal decision, not binding on higher courts, and its reasoning on 'no fundamental breach' has been overtaken by later Supreme Court authority.

adverse.title: L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav
adverse.principle: The insurer bears a heavy burden to prove the licence was fake or invalid with cogent evidence. Mere non-production of the licence by the owner does not discharge this burden. The insurer must also prove that the owner knew the licence was fake.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this for the proposition that the insurer must lead positive evidence (RTO verification, investigator's report properly proved) to establish that the licence was invalid. They will argue that if the insurer fails to examine the RTO official or produce a verified report, the breach is not proved. They will also argue that the owner's due diligence is a defence — if the owner believed the driver had a licence, there is no 'fundamental breach'.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In this case, the insurer alleged the licence was 'fake' but failed to lead cogent evidence — the investigation report was not properly proved. In your case, if the driver had NO licence at all (not a fake one), the burden is different: the absence of a licence can be proved through the charge sheet (which will note 'no licence'), the owner's failure to produce it despite opportunity, and the driver's non-appearance or admission. The court in doc_005 itself noted the insurer must prove 'fundamental breach' — complete absence of any licence is inherently a fundamental breach. Additionally, the recent Supreme Court in Hind Samachar (cited in doc_005) confirms that the owner must exercise due diligence — if the owner simply handed the truck to someone without checking, that is negligence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this for the straightforward proposition that even with no valid licence, the insurer must pay and recover — they will argue this is the settled law and the insurer cannot avoid payment altogether. They will rely on the court's citation of S. Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports the pay-and-recover framework, not complete exoneration. It confirms the insurer's right to recover from the owner. The risk is low because it does not undermine the defence — it merely confirms the remedy is pay-and-recover, which is exactly what we are prepared for. The court applied S. Iyyapan and Swaran Singh and held that even with no valid licence, the insurer must pay and recover. This is consistent with our position.
adverse.quote: Even if the offending vehicle was being driven by the driver having no valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further insurer has a right to recover the amount of compensation from the insured i.e. owner of the offending vehicle.

priority_arguments: 1. The driver had NO valid driving licence at all — this is a 'fundamental breach' under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act, as held in Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) and Satto (doc_033). The complete absence of a licence is the strongest category of breach, distinguishable from cases involving expired licences (doc_034) or missing endorsements (doc_032).

2. The burden of proving the breach is on the insurer, but it is discharged by: (a) the charge sheet showing the driver had no licence; (b) the owner's failure to produce the driving licence despite opportunity; (c) the driver's non-appearance or admission. See doc_024 where the Tribunal drew an adverse inference from non-production. Also examine the RTO official to verify the licence status.

3. Even if the Tribunal directs pay-and-recover (which is the likely outcome), the insurer must secure an express recovery right against the owner. The Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) confirms this is available even for Act policies. The recovery right should be explicitly recorded in the award.

4. If the deceased was a gratuitous passenger in the truck (not the owner of goods or his representative), argue that the insurer has no statutory liability at all under Section 147 — see doc_014 (Shivlal) and doc_029 (Minor Mahesh). In that case, even pay-and-recover may not be available (doc_029).

5. Quantum: If liability is established, argue for deduction of 50% towards personal expenses if the deceased was a bachelor (Sarla Verma), and no future prospects if the deceased was self-employed above 40. Use the compute_quantum tool for precise figures once the deceased's particulars are known.
strategy.compensation_range: If liability is established, the compensation will depend on the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. Without those facts, a precise range cannot be given. However, the corpus shows typical awards for death claims range from approximately Rs. 5-25 lakhs depending on the deceased's income and age. Use compute_quantum once the deceased's particulars are known.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. Key variables: (1) monthly income (to be proved by the claimants); (2) age of deceased (determines multiplier); (3) number of dependents (determines dependency deduction — 1/3rd for 2-3 dependents, 1/4th for 4+, 1/2 for 1 dependent); (4) future prospects (25% if self-employed below 40, 40% if employed below 40, 15% if self-employed between 40-50, 10% if between 50-60, nil if above 60); (5) conventional heads (Rs. 70,000 under Pranay Sethi as updated).
risks: 1. The Tribunal will almost certainly direct pay-and-recover rather than complete exoneration — this is the near-certain outcome for third-party claims. The insurer should be prepared for this and ensure the recovery right is explicitly recorded in the award.

2. If the claimants prove that the owner made reasonable enquiries and believed bona fide that the driver had a licence, the breach may not be 'fundamental' — see doc_005 (Bindudevi) citing Hind Samachar. The insurer must probe whether the owner exercised due diligence in employing the driver.

3. If the deceased was travelling as an owner of goods or his authorised representative in the truck, the insurer may still be liable under Section 147 — the 'gratuitous passenger' defence (doc_014, doc_029) may not apply.

4. The claimant will cite S. Iyyapan (doc_032) and Swaran Singh to argue that the insurer must pay even with no licence — this is correct law, but the insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner. The risk is that the Tribunal may not grant recovery rights if the breach is not proved to the requisite standard.

5. If the insurer fails to lead proper evidence (e.g., examining the RTO official, producing the driving licence verification report, or proving the charge sheet), the breach may not be held proved — see doc_005 where the insurer's investigation report was not properly exhibited.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: The matter will proceed before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be: (a) a finding that the driver had no valid driving licence, constituting a fundamental breach of policy conditions; (b) an order directing the insurer to pay the award and recover the same from the insured owner (pay-and-recover); (c) alternatively, if the facts permit (e.g., gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle), complete exoneration. The insurer should also consider filing a separate recovery proceeding against the owner after satisfying the award.
